JBL Go 4 vs Sony SRS-XB100: Which Tiny Bluetooth Speaker Should You Buy?

The JBL Go 4 ($31.95 on Amazon) is the modern pocket speaker with Bluetooth 5.3 and app EQ. The Sony SRS-XB100 ($33.06 on Amazon) doubles the battery life and floats. We put them head-to-head to find out which one you should actually buy.

Published November 2026 · Based on verified Amazon product data and real customer outcomes

If you want a speaker small enough to toss in a backpack pocket, the decision almost always comes down to two names: JBL and Sony. The JBL Go 4 is the fourth generation of the world's most popular ultra-portable speaker, and the Sony SRS-XB100 is its direct rival — a super-compact speaker that has been quietly dominating the budget "shower speaker" category for years.

Here's the thing: right now they cost almost the same. We saw the JBL Go 4 at $31.95 and the Sony SRS-XB100 at $33.06 on Amazon as we wrote this (the Go 4 lists for $49.95, so JBL is currently discounted well below MSRP). Both are IP67 waterproof and dustproof, both take USB-C, and both have a built-in mic for calls.

They're trying to solve the same problem with very different priorities. JBL went for newer wireless tech and a smarter sound tuning system. Sony went for raw battery life, a physical carry strap, and a speaker that literally floats. We compared the verified specs, feature sets, and real-world reviewer patterns to answer the question: which one should you buy?

Quick Verdict

Buy the JBL Go 4 if: You want the better-sounding speaker at your desk, in the dorm, or on a shelf. Bluetooth 5.3 connects faster and holds a steadier link than the Sony's 5.0, the JBL Portable app gives you a real adjustable EQ (the XB100 has no app at all), and JBL's tuning squeezes more usable volume out of the tiny cabinet. It's also the more modern design, built partly from recycled materials.

Buy the Sony SRS-XB100 if: Battery life is your #1 concern. The XB100 runs up to 16 hours per charge versus the Go 4's 7 — more than double. It also floats in water, has a built-in carry strap you can loop over a backpack strap or tent pole, and at roughly 274 g it's a solid, simple puck with zero app setup required.

Our pick: The JBL Go 4. At the same money, you get newer Bluetooth, an EQ app, Auracast speaker-linking, and — in most head-to-head sound tests — clearer, louder audio that doesn't distort at volume. The Sony's battery is impressive, but a speaker's job is sound, and the Go 4 does that job better.

Our Pick 🏆 JBL Go 4 Ultra-Portable Bluetooth Speaker

Check current price (as of November 21, 2026 — MSRP $49.95) on Amazon

The Go 4 is barely bigger than a deck of cards but somehow produces real JBL Pro Sound — punchy, full, and not the tinny rattle you'd expect at this size. The single full-range driver with its waveguide tuning fills a dorm room or a kitchen easily, and the bass (while modest, physically) is tighter than anything else in the sub-$35 bracket.

The generational upgrades are meaningful. Bluetooth 5.3 means near-instant pairing and a more stable connection through walls. Auracast lets you link the Go 4 to other Auracast-capable JBL speakers for bigger coverage. And the JBL Portable app adds a true graphic EQ — you can dial in more bass for outdoors or tame the treble for podcasts without touching a playlist.

It's IP67 rated — fully dustproof and survives being dunked — charges over USB-C, and JBL builds it partly from recycled plastic and fabric. The 7-hour battery is the honest weak spot: it'll cover a day of classes or a long shower session, but it won't cover a weekend camping trip without a power bank.

Key specs: Bluetooth 5.3, IP67 waterproof + dustproof, up to 7-hour battery, USB-C charging, speakerphone with voice pickup, Auracast wireless speaker linking, adjustable EQ via JBL Portable app, made with recycled materials.

🔋 Sony SRS-XB100 Wireless Bluetooth Speaker

Check current price on Amazon

The XB100 is Sony's answer to "what if we made a pocket speaker that never dies?" It runs up to 16 hours on a charge — the number that wins this spec sheet — and it charges over modern USB-C. At around 274 g it has a reassuring heft, and its Sound Diffuser waveguide spreads the mono signal evenly, so it doesn't sound like it's coming from one tiny corner.

The practical touches are where Sony shines. A built-in fabric carry strap lets you hang it from a shower caddy, backpack, or tent line — JBL gives you nothing to hang on. And because it's sealed air-tight, the XB100 floats, which is a genuinely useful trick for pool days, lake houses, and households with kids who fling things into bathtubs.

The trade-offs: Bluetooth 5.0 (two generations older — pairing is fine, but range and stability in busy apartments are measurably behind 5.3), no companion app and no EQ, and a sound that leans warmer and softer. It can stereo-pair with a second XB100, but only with itself, not with other brands.

Key specs: Bluetooth 5.0, IP67 waterproof + dustproof (floats), up to 16-hour battery, USB-C charging, hands-free calling, built-in carry strap, Sound Diffuser waveguide, wireless stereo pairing (XB100 + XB100), approx. 274 g.

Sound Quality: Where the Go 4 Wins

This is the category that decides the comparison. The Sony XB100 is a perfectly honest little mono speaker: warm mids, gentle highs, and a single passive radiator that adds a soft thump when you ask for bass. Its Sound Diffuser cone genuinely helps — the sound spreads out instead of pointing at you — and for podcasts, YouTube, and background music it's more than fine.

But the JBL Go 4 is the last generation of a product that's been acoustically refined four times over. Its tuning gives you noticeably more output before distortion, crisper treble, and a bass response that keeps its shape at 70-80% volume instead of getting muddy. Across the published head-to-head reviews and thousands of customer photos-in-context we looked at, the pattern is consistent: the Go 4 sounds bigger than the Sony at the same listening level.

And the JBL Portable app's EQ changes the math on the one area where the Sony's sound is genuinely safer. Want a warmer, calmer tone for late-night listening? You can dial that in. The XB100 gives you whatever Sony decided, forever.

Battery: Where the Sony Wins (By a Lot)

7 vs 16 hours isn't a tie, and we're not going to pretend otherwise. If you're buying a speaker for a weekend of camping without outlets, a long travel day, or you simply hate charging things, the Sony is the rational choice — it will outlast the JBL by more than a full charge cycle, every time.

The honest framing: most people charge a desktop-sized speaker from the same USB-C cable that's already behind their monitor. The Go 4's 7 hours covers a full day of intermittent use for most people. But "most people" isn't everyone — and if you know you're a road-tripper or a festival regular, the Sony's spec directly targets your use case.

💡 Tip: Both speakers charge over USB-C with the same cable as a modern phone. If you're splitting hairs on price, check the current price on both listings before deciding — the Go 4 fluctuates between $29 and $49 depending on sale cycles, and it's currently below the Sony.

Design Details That Matter Day-to-Day

The Sony's carry strap is underrated. Being able to hang the speaker on a shower rail, hook it to a backpack strap, or dangle it from a tree branch changes where you'll actually use it. The Go 4 has a small slot you can thread a lanyard through (sold separately), which is a weak substitute.

Floating is Sony's party trick, but a useful one: drop the XB100 in the pool and you fish it out and keep listening. Drop the Go 4 in and it sinks (it survives IP67 immersion, but it doesn't swim).

On connectivity, JBL's Bluetooth 5.3 is the newer standard with better power efficiency and more stable links through obstructions — you'll feel it in a crowded dorm or apartment where 5.0 speakers stutter on video sync. Auracast also future-proofs the Go 4 for linking with newer JBL speakers, while Sony keeps you inside its own pairing ecosystem.

Who Should Buy Which?

Buy the JBL Go 4 if this speaker lives on your desk, your nightstand, your shower shelf, or your daypack, and you care about how it actually sounds. At $31.95 — nearly $18 under MSRP — the Go 4 is simply the better piece of audio engineering for the money, and the app EQ plus Bluetooth 5.3 keep it feeling modern for years. It is our pick.

Buy the Sony SRS-XB100 if it's going places with no chargers: camping, beach days, long road trips, or as the speaker you keep in a bag for weeks at a time. Sixteen hours, a strap, and a floating body make it the most capable "set it and forget it" tiny speaker on the market.

Final Word

For most buyers, most rooms, and — right now — the lower price, the JBL Go 4 is the one we'd hand to a friend. Better sound, newer wireless, real EQ. The Sony SRS-XB100 is the specialist: buy it when runtime and the outdoors matter more than fidelity.
